SOURCE: Chapter 6 "Improving Reliability", Valliappa Lakshmanan and Hannes Hapke, Generative AI Design Patterns, O'Reilly, 2025 (book chapter; the PDF is a web print of the O'Reilly learning page).
File: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/03-agentic-foundations/sources/lakshmanan-hapke-genai-design-patterns-ch06-improving-reliability.pdf

COVERAGE: The PDF has 1 page, a single long web print, so "page" cannot cite anything. I cite extraction line numbers (L) instead, from /tmp/ch6.txt. I read all 71,864 chars, lines 1-1320, to the end. Code blocks come out after the prose, in order, with long lines truncated by the print. Footnote markers are lost; the footnote texts are at L1051-1064. There is no reference list, only inline author-year credits.

PATTERNS (Table 6-1, L959)
- Pattern 17 LLM-as-Judge
- Pattern 18 Reflection
- Pattern 19 Dependency Injection
- Pattern 20 Prompt Optimization

MEASURED VERSUS QUOTED: The chapter has no benchmark, no agreement-with-human figures and no statistics. Every number is either a single illustrative run by the authors (n=1) or an instruction in a prompt. No number comes from other work. Papers are credited by name only, never with a result.

CLAIMS (ranked)

Pattern 17, LLM-as-Judge (L19-379)

1. The pattern is three options that build on each other: a prompted rubric, an ML model over the judge's rubric scores, and a fine-tuned judge.
 - number: none
 - setup: You usually start with prompting. The ML option needs historical outcome data. The fine-tune option replaces the LLM with Adapter Tuning (Pattern 15), trained on human-expert scores from the same rubric.
 - quote: "Both the ML and fine-tuning approaches incorporate prompting—very often, you'll start with the prompting approach and then improve LLM-as-Judge by either ML or fine-tuning." (L82-84)
 - where: L80-87, L158-200
 - The ML option has three steps: write the rubric, collect historical outcomes (for example, whether a purchase came within "say, 30 days"), then train a classifier on the rubric scores. The authors say it "will discount any criteria that don't matter or on which the LLM is inconsistent (as long as you don't overfit, of course)" (L184-186).

2. Consistency tactics: temperature zero, caching, expanded rubric anchors, self-contained inputs, coarse scores, multiple criteria, multiple judges.
 - number: none (a 1-5 scale is called "usually OK")
 - quote: "a score range of 1 to 5 is usually OK, but the inconsistency problem becomes more acute if you set the range to 1 to 10 or 1 to 100. Taking this to the logical extreme, you'll get the best results from LLM-as-Judge if you can pose the score as a binary (yes or no) question." (L290-294)
 - quote: "nailing down the generation is not enough because you do want similar outputs to receive similar scores." (L285-286)
 - also: "Multiple criteria ... this is a form of CoT (Pattern 13)"; few-shot examples calibrate each criterion; one reference result can keep scores consistent. (L295-302)
 - "LLM-as-jury" means multiple LLMs, each in a stakeholder role. "Polling" means jury plus binary questions. (L303-311)
 - The authors give no measured effect for any of these tactics.

3. Judges are lenient, so do not rank two items by comparing their separate scores. Compare them directly instead.
 - number: none for the pattern itself (the logo example gives 0.9 vs 0.9, see Pattern 18)
 - quote: "LLMs tend to be extremely lenient with scores—like professors who give every student A's and B's. This, combined with LLMs' nondeterministic nature, means that you should avoid comparing the output scores for two pieces of content to determine a ranking. Instead, it's usually better to have your LLM-as-Judge compare the two pieces directly." (L313-318)
 - Other remedies: group-normalised scores, as in DeepSeek's GRPO ("each response is assigned a score that is normalized by the average score of the group", L322-323), or use the scores only to flag problems. The RAG example is "context loss, which scores 0 as opposed to the usual 0.95" (L327). That 0.95 is an illustrative figure with no setup given.

4. Bias list: self-bias, perplexity preference, length bias, positional bias.
 - number: none
 - quote: "LLMs tend to offer overly favorable scores when evaluating their own responses. This is called self-bias, and because of this, it's usually better to use a different LLM for evaluation than the LLM that was used to produce the content." (L330-333)
 - quote: "they tend to prefer well-written text (specifically, text with lower perplexity)—even if it is inaccurate—over badly written but accurate text." (L334-336)
 - Length and position: "LLMs may also favor lengthy reviews over concise ones", "may miss information that's located in the middle of lengthy text, and they tend to favor information at the beginning or end" (L337-340). No numbers and no citations for these claims.
 - Small fine-tuned judges are suggested as an alternative: PandaLM, and PatronusAI for multimodal or industry-specific metrics (L342-346).

5. Asking for a justification may hurt judge accuracy and bias mitigation (hedged).
 - number: none
 - quote: "There is some evidence that doing this, while offering interpretability, generally has a negative impact on the model's evaluation performance and bias mitigation." (L351-353)
 - The authors give no citation at that point. Footnote 2 (L1055) points to Wang et al., "Improving LLM-as-a-Judge Inference with the Judgment Distribution". Because the footnote markers were lost, that link is inferred from the footnote's position, so verify it.
 - Alternative if you do not need explanations: "take the probability-weighted mean score of the generated distribution (instead of choosing the most likely score...). Just be careful, as this interacts in somewhat weird ways with a CoT approach." (L354-357)

6. Design guidance: choose the score type by how it will be used, and make criteria a proxy for outcomes or KPIs.
 - Binary is best for decisions: "if you plan to make a decision based on the output of the model, a binary value is best" (L147-149).
 - If humans use the scores, ask for explanations.
 - "try to make the scoring criteria a proxy for either the outcome or the KPIs" and "watch out for adversarial actors trying to game the metrics" (L362-364).
 - Preprocess inputs to be self-contained, for example include enough conversation turns and summarize the agent's answers (L109-112).
 - Rubrics should anchor each score level (L116-132: for example "1 if any information in the summary misrepresents the article / 5 if all statements ... are grounded").
 - Traditional methods fail for open-ended output: outcome measurement is confounded, human evaluation is costly and biased, and BLEU/ROUGE "fail to capture semantic meaning, nuance, and factual correctness" (L66-67).

7. Worked example: scoring arguments in a Washington State voters' guide, with GPT-4o-mini.
 - number: none reported; the text shows only one "Understandable: 4" item (L272).
 - setup: 1-5 scale with five criteria (voter-centred, pyramid structure, understandable, clarity of call to action, caters to undecided), zero-shot, one run. Prompting was chosen because ML/fine-tuning "will require a lot of statistical rigor" (L240-242).
 - No validation against human judgment is shown.

Credited work (L366-379)
- Bai et al. (2023) call it "Language-Model-as-an-Examiner". The authors say this is the first academic mention they found.
- Shankar et al. (2024) cover alignment and consistency.
- Balog, Metzler and Qin (2025) cover biases.
- Hamel Husain (2024) and Eugene Yan (2025) are named practitioners.
- Gu et al. (2025) wrote the survey.
- Deployments named: DoorDash (Dasher support), AWS (Bedrock model evaluation), Acrolinx (brand-voice guardrails). No numbers.
- Pattern 17 also builds on Patterns 5, 10, 13, 14, 15 and 16 of the same book.

Pattern 18, Reflection (L380-559)

8. Reflection means generate, then critique, then regenerate with a modified prompt, repeated until a quality bar is met.
 - number: none
 - quote: "The evaluator doesn't just provide a score; it provides a critique explaining how the response falls short." (L403-404)
 - The evaluator can be an LLM, an external tool or a human. The authors note "there's no reason why the evaluation has to be done by an LLM at all" (L387-388).
 - Variations: a max-attempts cap, and "exactly one retry is quite common because it lets you avoid having to determine what 'good enough' means" (L412-413). A single retry can be zero-shot CoT, asking the model to reconsider. In conversational systems the critic is one participant, with an AutoGen code snippet (L416-420).

9. Threshold failure in the authors' logo run: a weighted rubric score could not separate a good logo from an average one. Their fix was one fixed round of critique.
 - number: 0.9 for both logos
 - setup: Authors' own run, n=1 each. Evaluator is Claude Sonnet 3.7 (the extraction prints "Claude Sonnet 3.7"). Generator is Gemini 2.0, a multimodal LLM. Rubric is five 1-5 criteria with a weighted average (formula in CODE). The two logos are Pydantic's real logo and a generated sushi-restaurant logo.
 - quote: "The PydanticAI logo received a score of 0.9, but so did the sushi logo. This is, surprisingly, a common problem—since LLMs tend to be lenient scorers, it's hard to come up with a rubric that can distinguish between a 'good enough' design and a great one." (L465-468)
 - where: L462-470
 - The caption says Pydantic company, but the text says "PydanticAI logo". The source is inconsistent here.

10. Reflection costs extra calls and latency, and its value depends on the use case.
 - number: none
 - quote: "At the time of writing, many frontier model API providers are struggling with availability. You often need to have a retry strategy just to get the first call to succeed, and Reflection, by introducing the need to make multiple calls to accomplish a task, can increase tail latency beyond acceptable limits." (L520-523) This is a POINT-IN-TIME statement.
 - Code generation justifies multiple stages, with compilers and sandboxes as external evaluators. Chatbots and real-time game engines may not tolerate the latency (L524-534).
 - Beam-search-style variant: draft several candidates, edit all, prune after each step (L535-539).
 - Use a different LLM as evaluator to avoid self-bias: "we used Gemini to create the logo images and Claude to generate the critique" (L545-546).
 - Other reasons given: quality and robustness, mitigating reasoning and planning limits, transparency (L501-512). Andrew Ng's four agentic patterns are mentioned, with Reflection as one (L499).

Credited work (L550-559)
- Flavell (1979), metacognition.
- Rabinowitz et al. (2018), theory of mind via RL.
- Shinn et al. (2023), Reflexion.
- Madaan et al. (2023), self-refine.
- Asai et al. (2023), Self-RAG.
- Dou et al. (2024), fewer code bugs.
- Amazon uses a validation LLM to check product listings. No numbers.

Pattern 19, Dependency Injection (L560-710)

11. Make every step of an LLM chain swappable by passing it as a function argument, so each step can be tested with a mock for the others.
 - number: none
 - Problem list: nondeterminism, models change on unknown schedules and "the longer and more detailed your prompts, the more brittle they are", and code must be LLM-agnostic (L567-585). Portable APIs and frameworks "don't help make your prompts portable" (L583-585).
 - The solution is mockable steps with the same signature. The default argument is the real LLM function (the `improvement_chain` snippet in CODE).
 - Testing means assertions on structured outputs: at least 4 improvements, and the chosen change is in the list. A difflib check requires that the modified lines are in a 1-5 range (L629-630, L659-663). LLM-as-Judge can add nuanced checks. Run the tests before every deployment or commit. This is explicit framing against "vibe checking" (L623-628).
 - Python note: `python -O` turns assertions off in production and Pytest gives rich failure info (L682-687).

12. Caveats
 - Hard-coded mocks "can be difficult to get right as the interaction between the steps increases" (L696-699). You can also mock external tools.
 - POINT-IN-TIME: "At the time of writing, Dependency Injection is not supported natively by any of the GenAI frameworks, although Pydantic comes close with dependency injection of prompts and tools into agents, but not of the agents themselves." (L707-710) This has likely dated.
 - Builds on: Fowler (2024) and Spring-style frameworks.

Pattern 20, Prompt Optimization (L711-946)

13. Four components: a pipeline, a dataset (as small as one example), an evaluator, and an optimizer. The optimizer returns the pipeline with the best-scoring prompt per step. It is meant to be rerun whenever the model or another dependency changes. (L738-762)
 - quote: "every time the LLM version changes, you can rerun the pipeline, get a prompt that performs well across many books, and continue on. Your code itself doesn't have prompts." (L909-911)
 - Prompt libraries and versioning do not solve this: "you'll still have to experiment manually whenever your dependencies change" (L916-917). The authors still call them good practice, and deliberately did not list them as patterns.

14. Measured example, single run, evaluated by the same style of LLM judge:
 - number: 0.63 for the baseline DSPy rewrite; 0.74 for BestOfN with N=10, threshold 0.95
 - setup: Task is rewriting the back-cover blurb of the authors' own book, Machine Learning Design Patterns. Model is claude-3-7-sonnet-latest through DSPy. The module is a ChainOfThought pipeline of extract then improve. The reward is a reference-comparison judge scoring from -1 to 1, with 0.1 subtracted per line over a maximum (aggregate formula in CODE). The judge LLM is the same one (no separate judge model is configured). One run, n=1, and no human validation. The authors say the rewritten text was "much more appealing" but also that "elite AI teams" made them cringe.
 - quote: "The fitness score for the rewritten one is 0.63, which indicates a considerable improvement over the original." (L843-844) and "When we did this, we got a score of 0.74—which is higher than the 0.63 we got earlier." (L881)
 - where: L843, L881
 - Cost: best-of-N means "you have to run inference 10 times" (L894-895).
 - Few-shot alternative: BootstrapFewShot with a dataset of examples. The authors' explanation: "if you have 10 examples, you'll pick 3 of them to serve as examples and then evaluate how well this prompt works on the remaining 7" (L898-900). That is an illustration, not a result. No result number is given for it. If thousands of examples exist, DSPy can fine-tune instead (L929-931).

15. Judge design lesson: use a reference-comparison judge, not absolute scores.
 - quote: "If one of the blurbs is rated 0.89 and the other is rated 0.90, it's difficult to trust in the improvement. You'll get better results if you give the LLM the original text as a reference blurb and ask it to compare the rewritten blurb to the original" (L837-840)
 - A footnote says the scoring-by-itself problem "is exactly what happened when we evaluated each blurb by itself" (L1063-1064). This is an anecdote, not a measurement.

16. Ties between the patterns (the link back to the primary target note)
 - quote: "You can export the prompts and human feedback to a dataset to build an assessment prompt (LLM-as-Judge) by using Prompt Optimization." (L939-940)
 - The captured prompts, even without human feedback, can build a dataset for post-training a task-specific LLM (L941-943).
 - POINT-IN-TIME: "other frameworks (besides DSPy) that support Prompt Optimization are AdalFlow and PromptWizard. PydanticAI is considering supporting it." (L932-934) Likely dated.
 - Builds on: DSPy, Khattab et al., Stanford, 2023, "DSPy: Compiling Declarative Language Model Calls into Self-Improving Pipelines" (L945-947).

LIMITS
- There are no experiments with a control group. Every result is a single illustrative run, with no judge-versus-human agreement, no variance across runs and no measured effect of any consistency tactic.
- Bias claims (self-bias, length, position, perplexity, justification hurting accuracy) are asserted with no citation attached at that point and no numbers. Treat them as practitioner folklore backed by the field, and cite the primary papers instead if the note needs evidence. The "some evidence" claim in item 5 is the weakest.
- The logo and voter-guide examples are subjective tasks with no ground truth.
- The authors concede mock data is hard to get right, that Reflection's value depends on latency and cost, and that threshold choice is hard (hence one-shot reflection).
- Point-in-time items:
  - API availability struggles (L520).
  - No GenAI framework natively supports DI (L707).
  - Prompt-optimizer framework list (L932).
  - Model names: GPT-4o-mini, Claude Sonnet 3.7, Gemini 2.0, claude-3-7-sonnet-latest.
- No coverage of position-swap debiasing, judge calibration against human labels (beyond the fine-tune option), or pairwise-versus-pointwise evidence. The pairwise recommendation is asserted, not measured.

BUILDS ON
Bai et al. 2023; Shankar et al. 2024; Balog, Metzler and Qin 2025; Husain 2024; Yan 2025; Gu et al. 2025; Wang et al. (judgment distribution, footnote 2, year not printed); DeepSeek GRPO (no year or citation); PandaLM; PatronusAI; Flavell 1979; Rabinowitz et al. 2018; Shinn et al. 2023 (Reflexion); Madaan et al. 2023 (Self-Refine); Asai et al. 2023 (Self-RAG); Dou et al. 2024; Andrew Ng's agentic patterns (no year); Fowler 2024 (DI); Khattab et al. 2023 (DSPy); Koenig/Lampson/Wheeler aphorism (decorative).

CODE (short, verbatim; line numbers in /tmp/ch6.txt)
- Judge prompt and temperature setting. The rubric prompt is at L93-104. The temperature setting:
  agent = Agent(CLAUDE, model_settings = {"temperature": 0 # for LLM-as-Judge}) (L1081-1084)
- Weighted logo score (L1086-1091):
  return (10 * self.clarity + 10 * self.appropriateness + 30 * self.no_conflicts + 30 * self.clean_design + 20 * self.easy_to_recognize) / 500.0
- Injectable chain (L1187-1198):
  def improvement_chain(in_text, critique_fn=critique, improve_fn=improve): c = critique_fn(in_text); assert_critique(c); improved = improve_fn(in_text, c); assert_improvement(improved, in_text, c); return improved
- Mock use (L1217): improved = improvement_chain(mldp_text, critique_fn=mock_critique...)
- DSPy aggregate score with length penalty (L1272-1284): topic and contents weighted 10 each, plus the sum of objective scores, divided by (20 + number of objectives), minus 0.1 per line over the limit, floored at 0.
- Best-of-N optimizer (L1291-1296): dspy.BestOfN(module=BlurbPipeline(), N=10, reward_fn=score_reward, threshold=0.95)
- Few-shot optimizer (L1304): optimizer = BootstrapFewShot(metric=evaluate_blurb); optimized_pipeline = optimizer.compile(BlurbPipeline(), trainse...) (truncated by the print)
- The reference-comparison judge signature BlurbScore (L1259-1269) is worth keeping as the pairwise-with-reference pattern, with scores from -1 to 1.

FIGURES (caption listing only; the PDF is one page, so p1 for all, and I did not view the images)
- Fig 6-1: three approaches to LLM-as-Judge (prompting, ML, fine-tuning). Best candidate for the judge note: it shows how the options build on each other.
- Fig 6-2: Reflection adds an intermediate critiquing step to the typical LLM usage pattern. Candidate for the reflection note.
- Fig 6-3: Pydantic logo, the evaluator input.
- Fig 6-4: initial Gemini sushi logo.
- Fig 6-5: before and after one round of Reflection. Shows the effect, but it is a single qualitative example.
- Fig 6-6: replacing Step 1 with a mock. Candidate for the DI illustration.
- Fig 6-7: Prompt Optimization has a pipeline, a dataset, an evaluator and an optimizer. Candidate for the 08-prompt-optimization note.

PROBLEMS
- Single-page PDF, so no page citations are possible. Line numbers in /tmp/ch6.txt are my own and are not stable in the file.
- Code lines are truncated by the web print. The AutoGen snippet's elided header sits in the code dump, not inline.
- Footnote markers are missing. The mapping of footnote 2 (Wang et al.) to the "some evidence" sentence is inferred from position.
- The web print ends with site navigation text ("Explore Skills ...", chapter links). I ignored it. No embedded instructions found.
- I did not view the figure images.
